rationale: Asks what Seneca Falls reformers were doing by borrowing the Declaration's language; identifying the source's purpose (claiming the founding generation's liberty/equality ideals for women) -> 2.A; women's-rights convention of 1848 -> 4.11.
Asks how the Market Revolution changed how ordinary Americans lived and worked; explaining a development/process -> 1.B; commercial agriculture, wage labor, linked markets -> 4.5.
Asks what the Embargo Act exemplifies (a foreign-policy measure whose unintended result was manufacturing growth); identifying a historical concept -> 1.A; Jefferson-era embargo -> 4.2.

Explains how the cult of domesticity coexisted with Seneca Falls (the ideal constrained most women while a minority challenged it); explaining -> 1.B; framed around the 1848 women's-rights convention so 4.11, though the domestic ideal itself sits in 4.6.
Asks which conclusion the treaty image best supports (doubled territory by diplomacy); explaining how evidence supports a claim -> 3.D; Louisiana Purchase -> 4.2.
Asks what the Ograbme cartoon best reflects (the embargo hurt American merchants most); identifying a source's argument -> 3.A; Embargo Act -> 4.2.
Asks the outcome of the War of 1812 (stalemate that fueled nationalism and industry); explaining a development -> 1.B; War of 1812 -> 4.4.
Asks what the Purchase and the Embargo together exemplify (Jefferson exercising broad federal power against his small-government vision); identifying a concept -> 1.A; Jefferson era -> 4.2.

Relates the Roosevelt Corollary to the Monroe Doctrine (extension: warning to Europe becomes justification for U.S. intervention); explaining how one development relates to another -> 5.B; corollary/imperialism debates -> 7.2.
Asks what Monroe's 1823 message was as a document (a presidential policy statement aimed at Europe as much as Congress); identifying a source's purpose/audience -> 2.A; Monroe Doctrine -> 4.4.
Asks how the Dawes Act reduced Native landholding (allotments plus 'surplus' sales to whites); identifying the process -> 1.A; allotment policy -> 6.3.
Asks which conclusion the Dawes Act's 'surplus' provision best supports (it transferred land to white ownership whatever its stated aims); how evidence supports a claim -> 3.D; Dawes Act -> 6.3.
Asks what the Little Bighorn->reservations->Dawes->Wounded Knee sequence illustrates (a sustained federal campaign to confine and subdue); identifying the pattern -> 1.A; Plains wars -> 6.3.
Asks why railroads mattered in the Plains conflicts (they moved troops and supplies rapidly); explaining a process -> 1.B; railroad-driven western economic development -> 6.2.
Asks what the Wounded Knee burial photo is evidence of (the violent endpoint of the conquest campaign); how evidence supports a claim -> 3.D; Wounded Knee -> 6.3.

Explains the link between industrialization and Native policy (railroads needed steel, steel needed coal/iron, the Plains were needed for all three); explaining -> 1.B; content bridges 6.6 and 6.2 -- chose 6.2 since the land/resource demand is westward-expansion economics.
Asks how reservations and the Dawes Act differed (collective holding vs individual allotments plus 'surplus' sales); identifying the concept -> 1.A; Native land policy -> 6.3.

Asks which provides the strongest support for the land-transfer claim (the 'surplus' provision authorizing sales to settlers); identifying evidence used to support an argument -> 3.B; Dawes Act -> 6.3.

Asks what a historian must first consider about Sinclair's Jungle passage (he wrote as a reform-minded journalist aiming to shock readers into demanding change); identifying the source's purpose -> 2.A; muckraking -> 7.4.
Asks what Nixon was doing in the 1969 'silent majority' address (addressing a TV audience of voters, seeking support amid upheaval); identifying purpose/audience -> 2.A; Nixon-era politics -> 8.14.
Asks what The Liberator was as a source (an openly immediatist abolitionist journal, not neutral); identifying the source's purpose -> 2.A; abolitionism -> 4.11.

Asks what the Dawes Act's 'consent to sell' language is useful as evidence of (the legal mechanism moving reservation land onto the market); explaining the source's purpose/situation -> 2.B, though it also reads as identifying the mechanism (2.A).

Asks what to recognize about the Zimmermann telegram (a secret German cable revealing Berlin's intentions but saying nothing about American public opinion); how a source's nature limits its use -> 2.C; WWI diplomacy -> 7.5.
Asks what caution Carter's 1979 'crisis of confidence' address requires (a president's framing, not a neutral measure of belief); how purpose limits use -> 2.C; Carter era -> 8.14.

Asks what the Free Speech Movement was challenging from Savio's 'bodies upon the gears' speech (the university's ban on student political activity); identifying a source's claim -> 3.A; 1960s campus protest -> 8.12.
Asks why Vietnam dominated campus protest (the draft made it personal for college-age men); explaining a development -> 1.B; Vietnam War -> 8.8.
Evaluates the claim that Woodstock proves most youth joined the counterculture (the image is mistaken for the whole generation); how evidence refutes a claim -> 3.D; counterculture -> 8.12.
Asks what the counterculture was rejecting (the postwar package: careers, suburbs, conformity); identifying the concept -> 1.A; counterculture -> 8.12.
Asks why the generation gap became a political force (Nixon named the backlash and turned it into votes); explaining -> 1.B; 1960s political realignment -> 8.14.
Asks what the 'silent majority' backlash stood for (law and order, patriotism, traditional values); identifying the concept -> 1.A; conservative backlash -> 8.14.
Asks what rock music as the generation's common language shows (youth shared a culture across regions and campuses); identifying -> 1.A; youth culture -> 8.12.

Asks the historical connection between the 1964 Free Speech Movement and later antiwar protest (campus protest networks built in 1964 carried into the antiwar movement); explaining how developments relate -> 5.B; campus protest continuity -> 8.12.

Asks how the counterculture hardened the conservative coalition (it provoked a backlash around law and order and traditional values); explaining the causal mechanism -> 1.B; conservative resurgence -> 8.14.
Asks what Haight-Ashbury provided (a community living out the 'do your own thing' ethic in communes); identifying the concept -> 1.A; counterculture -> 8.12.
Asks what 'hippie' becoming a political insult shows (the cultural split had become a political weapon); identifying the claim's meaning -> 3.A; politicization of culture -> 8.14.

Asks what the ongoing culture wars imply about the 1960s (its cultural divisions outlasted the decade); identifying the continuity pattern -> 5.A, though explaining the 1960s-to-present relationship could be read as 5.B.
Asks what Silent Spring changed in American attitudes (postwar faith in chemical progress turned to suspicion); explaining -> 1.B; environmental movement -> 8.13.
Asks why the Santa Barbara spill, burning Cuyahoga, and Love Canal mattered politically (they made pollution visible, building demand for action); explaining -> 1.B; environmental politics -> 8.13.
Asks what the 20-million turnout on the first Earth Day demonstrated (environmental concern was a mass cause); identifying the claim the evidence supports -> 3.A; Earth Day -> 8.13.

Asks which shows the shared civil-rights/environmental toolkit in action (Earth Day's moral appeal and media event followed by federal legislation); identifying the pattern across movements -> 5.A; environmental movement -> 8.13.
Asks which law/year match is correct (Clean Air Act 1970); identifying a development -> 1.A; environmental statutes -> 8.13.

Asks what is wrong with the claim that Three Mile Island proves deadly radiation releases (almost no radiation escaped; fear froze construction); how evidence refutes a claim -> 3.D; nuclear accident -> 8.13.
Asks what drove the Sagebrush Rebellion (federal regulation threatened ranchers' and miners' livelihoods); explaining -> 1.B; anti-regulation backlash -> 8.13.

Asks what 'the same wall' means (both movements' reforms provoked organized conservative opposition); identifying the pattern across developments -> 5.A; environmentalism/civil-rights parallel -> 8.13.
Asks why environmentalism is 'the last' great liberal reform movement (the political tide turned against federal regulation after the 1970s); explaining -> 1.B; end of the liberal era -> 8.13.
Asks what Reagan's promise to shrink the EPA shows (the anti-regulation backlash had become governing policy); identifying the concept -> 1.A; 1980 environment politics -> 8.13.

Asks why the 'and readers' part of Carson's DDT finding mattered (it made pollution a human-health issue for a wider audience); identifying the significance of the source's claim -> 3.A, though reading it as an evidence-to-claim inference could be 3.D.
Asks why the great environmental statutes came in a 1970-73 burst (Earth Day and visible disasters created pressure Congress could not ignore); explaining -> 1.B; environmental legislation -> 8.13.
Asks what Love Canal demonstrated (industrial waste could threaten ordinary homes and families); identifying -> 1.A; toxic-waste scandal -> 8.13.
Asks why the burning Cuyahoga was politically powerful (a vivid, undeniable symbol of industrial pollution); identifying a non-text source's argument -> 3.A; environmental symbolism -> 8.13.
Asks what creating the EPA signaled (Washington took lasting responsibility for environmental protection); identifying -> 1.A; EPA -> 8.13.
Asks what the disaster->mobilization->legislation sequence shows (disaster built alarm, then mobilization, then legislation); identifying the pattern -> 1.A; movement mechanics -> 8.13.

Asks what broader 1960s change Silent Spring illustrates (the decade challenged confidence in science); identifying the broader pattern -> 5.A; topic is the environmental content itself (8.13) rather than general postwar culture (8.5) -- a judgment call.

Evaluates the claim that environmentalism 'copied the civil rights movement exactly' (shared toolkit, but 'exactly' overstates it); qualifying an argument with evidence -> 6.D; environmental movement -> 8.13.

Asks what US leadership of the Washington Naval Conference shows about 1920s foreign policy (limit war's costs but accept no binding commitments); identifying the historical situation -> 2.A; interwar foreign policy -> 7.11.

Asks why the unfinished USS Washington was destroyed (treaty terms required scrapping ships under construction); explaining how treaty evidence supports the interpretation -> 3.D, though it also reads as identifying supporting evidence (3.B).
Asks what explains Japan's turn against the treaty (resentment of its inferior 5:3 ratio as a racial insult); how evidence supports the claim -> 3.D; naval treaties -> 7.11.
Evaluates the claim the 5:5:3 ratios treated all signatories as equals (the numbers refute it: a hierarchy, not equality); how evidence refutes a claim -> 3.D; naval treaties -> 7.11.
Asks what the Four-Power and Nine-Power treaties show about US aims (Asian stability without binding commitments); identifying the concept -> 1.A; interwar Asia policy -> 7.11.
Asks what Kellogg-Briand required if a pledge was broken (nothing -- the pact had no enforcement mechanism); identifying the source's content -> 2.A; interwar treaties -> 7.11.
Asks what Kellogg's private dismissal of his own pact shows (the architect doubted paper promises could stop war); identifying the source's point of view -> 2.A; Kellogg-Briand -> 7.11.
Asks what Japan's unpunished 1931 Manchuria invasion shows (unenforced treaties cannot bind a determined power); identifying the concept -> 1.A; interwar foreign policy -> 7.11.

Asks what changed from the Roosevelt Corollary era (a claimed right to intervene became renouncing armed intervention under the Good Neighbor Policy); identifying the historical situation via the portrait/pledge -> 2.A; Good Neighbor Policy -> 7.11.
Asks why non-intervention became 1930s policy (Depression-era costs ended intervention; Washington wanted markets and cooperation); explaining -> 1.B; interwar Latin America policy -> 7.11.

Asks why the review makes Hughes rather than Harding the main disarmament actor (Hughes conceived and drove the diplomacy); identifying the source's (review's) point of view -> 2.A; Washington Conference -> 7.11.
Asks what explains improved US-Latin American relations (ending the occupations removed the main source of resentment); explaining -> 1.B; Good Neighbor Policy -> 7.11.
Asks what Congress concluded from the Nye Committee finding (economic ties caused the entanglement, so law must cut those ties); explaining -> 1.B; Neutrality Acts -> 7.11.

Asks what follows from the judgment that the Neutrality Acts misread 1917 (they attacked the wrong cause, since submarines caused the declaration); how evidence refutes a claim -> 3.D; Neutrality Acts -> 7.11.

Asks why impartial 'cash-and-carry' helped Britain and France (their sea power let them carry goods away, Germany's did not); explaining how the evidence supports the claim -> 3.D; Neutrality Acts -> 7.11.
Asks what the 1935-41 arc shows (the isolationist peak receded as war neared); identifying the concept -> 1.A; end of the neutrality era -> 7.11.
Asks where transcendentalists located truth (self-trust and nature, not institutions); identifying the source's point of view -> 2.A; transcendentalism -> 4.9.

Asks what later abolitionist and civil-rights citation of Thoreau shows (his principle outlived its moment and served later causes); explaining how one development relates to others -> 5.B; transcendentalist ideas -> 4.9.

Evaluates the claim that transcendentalism was historically unimportant because it was small (ideas mattered more than membership: the circle fueled three reform movements); how evidence modifies a claim -> 3.D; transcendentalism -> 4.9.

Asks what Fuller's Woman in the Nineteenth Century feeding the Seneca Falls generation shows (transcendentalist ideas fed the women's-rights movement); explaining the relationship -> 5.B; content bridges 4.9 and 4.11 -- chose 4.9 as the review's subject.
Asks what work Cole's Oxbow was doing (political work: American nature as morally superior to Europe's); identifying a non-text source's argument -> 3.A; Hudson River School -> 4.9.
Asks what tension Cole's Course of Empire reveals (celebration and elegy for a wilderness he feared would vanish); identifying the source's meaning -> 3.A; Cole -> 4.9.
Asks what Church's blockbuster-style touring shows (landscape art reached a wide audience beyond elites); identifying the source-based claim -> 3.A; landscape art -> 4.9.

Evaluates 'merely decorative' against Bierstadt's expansion-era western canvases (timing and subject show the paintings served expansion politics); supporting an argument with specific evidence -> 6.B, though explaining relationships among the evidence could be 6.C.

Asks what transcendentalist protest of an output-measured society shows about the Market Revolution era (critics saw human costs in the new market society); identifying -> 1.A; market society's cultural costs -> 4.6.

Asks what distinguishes the Second Great Awakening from transcendentalism (a mass outward revival versus a small circle's inward turn); identifying the contrast pattern -> 5.A; could be 4.10 since the Awakening is the comparator -- chose 4.9 as the review's subject.

Asks what the piracy of Irving's Sketch Book shows (real transatlantic demand for American writing); inferring a claim from the evidence -> 3.D, though it also reads as identifying the source's implication (3.A).
Asks what Cooper's 'vanishing Indian' stereotype shows (American literature carried the era's racial assumptions); identifying the source's meaning -> 3.A; Cooper -> 4.9.
Asks what Emerson was calling for in 'The American Scholar' (an intellectual life independent of European models); identifying the source's purpose -> 2.A; literary nationalism -> 4.9.

Asks what pattern literary nationalism as the 'cultural twin' of political/economic nationalism describes (nationalism ran through politics, economics, and culture); identifying the pattern -> 5.A; nationalism -> 4.9.
Asks what 'professional' implies about Irving and Cooper (they earned a living writing for an American market); identifying the concept -> 1.A; American writers -> 4.9.

Asks what post-1812 Americans finding 'American' in the landscape shows about culture's role (culture did nation-building work alongside canals and elections); supporting the argument with the review's evidence -> 6.B, though the stem mostly asks for identification.
Asks what the Wounded Knee mass-burial photo supports (some 250-300 Lakota dead, many women and children); how evidence supports the claim -> 3.D; Wounded Knee -> 6.3.
Asks what kind of resistance the Ghost Dance was (spiritual resistance: a religious movement of last hope); identifying the concept -> 1.A; Ghost Dance -> 6.3.
Asks what connects Sitting Bull's killing and Wounded Knee (fearful misreading of the Ghost Dance as a war dance drove both); explaining -> 1.B; December 1890 events -> 6.3.
Asks what the soldiers were doing when the Wounded Knee shooting started (disarming Big Foot's band); identifying the historical situation -> 2.A; Wounded Knee -> 6.3.
Asks the sound historical use of first-shot uncertainty (it limits first-shot claims; the one-sided outcome defines the event); how evidence constrains a claim -> 3.D; Wounded Knee -> 6.3.
Asks what the Hotchkiss guns and casualty pattern show (a one-sided slaughter rather than a battle); evidence to claim -> 3.D; Wounded Knee -> 6.3.

Evaluates the claim that all Native resistance ended in 1890 (qualifying: organized military resistance ended, leaving room for other forms); how evidence modifies an argument -> 3.D; end of the Indian wars -> 6.3.
Asks the theory behind the Dawes Act's design (private property would create farmers and dissolve tribalism); identifying the concept -> 1.A; allotment -> 6.3.
Asks what the 138M-to-48M acreage figures do to the reformers' liberation claim (they refute it); how evidence refutes -> 3.D; allotment outcomes -> 6.3.
Asks how allotment outcomes created conditions for the Ghost Dance (poverty and desperation in which renewal took hold); explaining the causal chain -> 1.B; allotment -> Ghost Dance -> 6.3.
Asks what American reaction the 1798 XYZ cartoon reflects (Federalist outrage at France and support for a hard line); identifying the source's point of view -> 2.A; XYZ Affair -> 3.10.

Asks what the XYZ Affair->Alien and Sedition Acts->KY/VA Resolutions sequence shows (a foreign crisis became a domestic fight over dissent and states' rights); explaining -> 1.B; early republic politics -> 3.10.
Asks what the 1591 Florida Indians planting engraving supports (farming was an established, organized part of Native life); identifying a source's claim -> 3.A; Native agriculture -> 1.2.
Asks why the three sisters system could support large settled communities (three food crops from the same field increased yields); explaining -> 1.B; Native agriculture -> 1.2.
Asks what the Cahokia/Tenochtitlan population comparison supports (maize farming could sustain very large cities in different regions); identifying the claim -> 3.A; maize-based urbanism -> 1.2.
Asks what explains Mississippian river-valley towns (fertile floodplain soils for maize surpluses); explaining -> 1.B; Mississippian settlement -> 1.2.

Asks what the Pueblo/Iroquois/Pacific Northwest examples together illustrate (societies shaped economies and ways of life around their environments); identifying the pattern -> 5.A; regional adaptation -> 1.2.
Asks why maize farming correlated with complex hierarchy (surpluses fed non-farming specialists like chiefs and priests); explaining -> 1.B; agriculture and complexity -> 1.2.
Asks what evidence challenges 'simple and unchanging' Native societies (Cahokia's mounds rivaled Europe's largest constructions); how evidence refutes a claim -> 3.D; Cahokia -> 1.2.
Asks what made permanent Iroquois village life possible (three sisters agriculture sustaining dense populations); explaining -> 1.B; Iroquois -> 1.2.
Asks what the Taos Pueblo image illustrates (a settled farming society suited to a dry environment); identifying the connection -> 5.A; Pueblo adaptation -> 1.2.
Asks what the two de Bry engravings together demonstrate (Native peoples combined farming with hunting); comparing the main ideas of two sources -> 3.C; Native subsistence -> 1.2.

Asks the most significant implication of Cahokia's pre-contact size (large complex societies arose in North America without European contact); identifying the historical context -> 4.A, though it also reads as a claim-about-evidence judgment.
Asks what follows from the mound-building evidence (leaders could organize and direct thousands); evidence to claim -> 3.D; Cahokia -> 1.2.
Asks which group/adaptation pairing is correct (Pueblo peoples -- farming adapted to the arid Southwest); identifying -> 1.A; regional adaptation -> 1.2.

Asks which comparison would best test the food-production-determines-complexity argument (a maize-farming chiefdom vs a non-farming foraging society in the same environment); using diverse evidence to test/qualify an argument -> 6.D; testing the thesis -> 1.2.

Asks why historians emphasize that Cahokia's mounds 'rivaled anything in Europe' (to show monumental building was achieved without Old World contact); explaining how the development is situated in broader context -> 4.B, though it also reads as explaining a historian's argument.
Asks what the three sisters' layered arrangement illustrates (crops combined so each uses a different layer of growing space); identifying -> 1.A; interplanting -> 1.2.

Asks the most important limitation of the de Bry engravings (a European artist who never visited, so they may reflect European assumptions); how a source's POV limits its use -> 2.C; sourcing Native evidence -> 1.2.
Asks for the best summary of environment vs social organization (farming regions dense and hierarchical; others smaller and mobile); identifying the pattern -> 5.A; adaptation -> 1.2.

Asks which question archaeological evidence can answer most reliably (whether the society could organize large-scale construction); judging what evidence can and cannot support -> 3.D, though it is fundamentally about limits of evidence.
Asks which group represents 'smaller and more mobile' (foraging bands in regions without maize agriculture); identifying -> 1.A; subsistence divide -> 1.2.
Asks what the encomendero owed in return (Christian instruction for the Native community); identifying the concept -> 1.A; encomienda -> 1.5.
Asks how Las Casas's reformist purpose shapes his passage (he stresses Spanish greed and cruelty to make reform seem urgent); explaining the source's purpose -> 2.B; Las Casas -> 1.5.
Asks what the New Laws of 1542 did (limited the encomienda and forbade new grants); identifying -> 1.A; New Laws -> 1.5.

Asks what changed and what stayed the same in colonial labor (coerced labor continued, but shifted from Native peoples to enslaved Africans); explaining how developments relate -> 5.B; labor transition -> 1.5.

Asks the historical significance of the Valladolid debate (it shows the morality of conquest was openly contested in 1500s Spain); identifying the broader historical context -> 4.A, though 'significance' could be read as 4.B's situating work.
Asks which motive Las Casas identifies as the driving force (gold, and ambition and greed for quick wealth and status); identifying a claim in the source -> 3.A; Las Casas -> 1.5.
Asks what the 'mestiza' casta painting illustrates (the colonial regime carefully classified people according to ancestry); identifying the source's meaning -> 3.A; casta system -> 1.5.
Asks what the 'mulato' label reveals (the system also classified the children of enslaved Africans, assigning them a named place); identifying -> 3.A; casta system -> 1.5.
Asks what the dozens of 'cambujo'-style casta labels are evidence of (the drive to fix legal/social status by ancestry even as mixing continued); evidence to claim -> 3.D; casta system -> 1.5.
Asks what the asiento was (the Crown's monopoly contract for supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America); identifying the concept -> 1.A; asiento -> 1.5.

Asks the significance of Potosi silver (it financed Spanish state power and tied the Americas to the global economy); explaining -> 1.B; bridges 1.4 (global exchange) and 1.5 (forced mining labor) -- chose 1.4 since the item stresses global economic integration.

Asks how epidemic disease reshaped colonial labor (it created a labor shortage that pushed Spain to import enslaved Africans); explaining how developments relate -> 5.B; disease-to-slavery shift -> 1.5.
Asks how historians should use Las Casas (a critic's view whose claims must be weighed against his reformist purpose); how purpose limits use -> 2.C; sourcing Las Casas -> 1.5.
Asks what the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 was (a coordinated uprising under Pope that drove the Spanish out for over a decade); identifying -> 1.A; Pueblo Revolt -> 2.5.
Asks why the Pueblo Revolt succeeded (communities across many villages coordinated under Pope, striking simultaneously); explaining how the developments relate -> 5.B; revolt's success -> 2.5.

Asks what broader pattern the Pueblo Revolt illustrates as Native resistance (sustained opposition to coerced labor and mission control in the Spanish colonies); situating the development within a broader context -> 4.B; Native resistance -> 2.5.
Asks what the encomienda's history suggests about its religious justification (it covered forced labor that even many Spaniards found indefensible); identifying the concept -> 1.A; encomienda -> 1.5.
Asks what the New Laws' outcome illustrates (dependence on coerced labor outlasted any single reform); explaining the continuity -> 5.B; labor system -> 1.5.
Asks what the 'torna atras' label reveals (colonial elites feared mixing could reverse a family's whiteness and status); identifying -> 3.A; casta anxiety -> 1.5.
Asks what the sixteen-panel casta set indicates (classifying people by ancestry had become a systematic preoccupation); identifying -> 1.A; casta system -> 1.5.
Asks what the triangular trade was (three-way Atlantic commerce linking Europe, Africa, and the Americas); identifying the concept -> 1.A; triangular trade -> 2.4.

Asks what the 1740 Atlantic chart's focus on winds and sailing courses reveals (merchants depended on predictable wind patterns); identifying the source's meaning -> 3.A; transatlantic commerce -> 2.4.
Asks what the Brookes stowage diagram demonstrates (the trade treated enslaved people as cargo packed for maximum profit); evidence to claim -> 3.D; Middle Passage -> 2.4.
Asks which Middle Passage condition Equiano's account documents (the overcrowded, filthy, despairing conditions below deck); identifying a claim in the source -> 3.A; Middle Passage -> 2.4.
Asks which triangular-trade leg the Elmina embarkation engraving shows (Africa to the Americas, carrying enslaved people); identifying the connection -> 5.A; triangular trade -> 2.4.
Asks what mercantilism held (colonies existed to enrich the mother country through favorable trade balances); identifying the concept -> 1.A; mercantilism -> 2.4.
Asks what Mun says increases wealth (sell more to foreigners each year than you buy from them); identifying a claim in the source -> 3.A; mercantilism -> 2.4.

Asks what Mun's 200,000-pound 'net gain' bar represents (how much exports exceeded imports: the yearly gain in treasure); identifying the evidence used to support his argument -> 3.B, though it also reads as identifying what the evidence shows (3.D).
Asks the purpose of the Navigation Acts under mercantilism (make sure colonial trade profits enriched England rather than its rivals); explaining -> 1.B; Navigation Acts -> 2.4.

Asks what Navigation Acts plus salutary neglect illustrate (mercantilist law claimed control on paper while colonial merchants enjoyed wide freedom); explaining how developments relate -> 5.B; mercantilism in practice -> 2.4.
Asks which triangular-trade leg plantation sugar represents (Americas to Europe, carrying plantation products to market); identifying -> 1.A; triangular trade -> 2.4.
Asks what system Havana's importance rested on (the movement of American silver and goods through Spanish ports to Europe); identifying the connection -> 5.A; Spanish Atlantic system -> 2.4.
